title: LinkedIn Postings Graded on the Employer's Own Words | vitalii.no
description:
How a job-scoring pipeline stopped letting a generous AI talk itself past requirements it should have flagged, by making the model report facts instead of an opinion.

12.6% of a month's LinkedIn postings scored 70 or higher under a one-size-fits-all prompt, including a junior developer role that needs a CS degree and a project manager role that needs a master's plus years of consulting experience. The same prompt that correctly filtered other sources let LinkedIn postings through, because its language gate only fired on exact phrases like "fluent Norwegian" or "native speaker."

For LinkedIn postings only, a strict prompt now asks the model to report structured fields instead of a soft judgment: language required, years required versus years actually evidenced by paid work, education required versus education met, and any must-have requirement the profile doesn't back up. A gating function then applies deterministic caps in code from those fields — fluent Norwegian caps the score, an experience-years gap caps it further, a missing degree caps it again — with every gate decision written to the analysis record so the reasoning is auditable.

A dry run on 24 postings that had scored 60 or above went from 11 postings at 70+ down to zero, and from 6 postings at 80+ down to zero — the mean score across those postings dropped from 73 to 50.
